title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
description: Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating."At 74,
body: Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating."At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery."I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year."I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing"."[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics. Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

schema.headline: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'

title: Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in Canada luxury car theft syndicate
description: Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.They are accused of stea
body: Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa. Police in Peel, Ontario said they had recovered 96 high-value vehicles concealed in shipping containers. The vehicles, valued at $4.5m (£3.4m) were destined for export via Canadian ports. The trafficking of vehicles from North America and Europe to African countries has been a long-standing concern for law enforcement agencies. The suspects face 231 charges, with arrest warrants issued for others. Police say some of the accused may face deportation after their criminal proceedings are concluded.The arrests followed months of what police described as an "extensive auto theft investigation".The investigations began in March in partnership with Canada's border agency after police identified a warehouse allegedly being used to store stolen vehicles.Investigators believe the network was led by five people who coordinated the theft, transportation and export of the stolen vehicles, with the others playing supporting roles."Together, investigators linked the network to loading sites, container movements and the transportation of stolen re-VINed vehicles," the police said in a statement.Re-VINing is the illegal practice of altering the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) to conceal its identity and make it harder to trace.Canadian authorities have described organised vehicle theft as a growing threat, saying it was linked to wider criminal networks."Organised auto theft is a predatory business model run by transnational syndicates that terrorise families and fund broader criminal enterprises," Peel Regional Police Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich said.Last year, Interpol said more than 100 luxury vehicles stolen from Canada and European countries had been recovered, exposing a network involved in trafficking stolen cars to West Africa.In a separate operation the same year, Ghanaian security authorities recovered 43 luxury vehicles stolen from Europe and North America.They attributed the success of the operation to improved cooperation between national and international law enforcement agencies.

schema.headline: Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in Canada luxury car theft syndicate

title: Gunmen kill Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez
description: A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.Polic
body: A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.Police said gunmen on a motorbike ambushed Camilo Rodríguez, 50, as he was travelling in his car north of the capital, San José, on Monday afternoon.The independent reporter earlier said he had been receiving death threats from drug trafficking gangs. Local media reported that it was the first murder of a journalist in more than two decades in Costa Rica. It comes at a time when transnational crime gangs are increasing their presence in the country, driving up its formerly low homicide rate. The president of the Costa Rican Journalists' Association, Yanancy Noguera, said that "all evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica - a person who published information about organised crime in the country".Rodríguez had been working as a journalist for several decades, both in radio and in print. Most recently, he had been uploading videos to social media in which he named public figures such as judges, business people and politicians, which he alleged were corrupt or had ties to known drug traffickers.In one of his videos, he alleged that the home of Costa Rica's President, Laura Fernández, had been constructed by a company that he said had links to a criminal gang.Fernández, who categorically denied any wrongdoing, took the journalist to court, accusing him of defamation. Reacting to his murder in a video message, the president strongly condemned the attack, calling it "a stain on freedom of expression". She added that she had instructed police to do their utmost to "punish Camilo's murderers".Rodríguez had also tried to stand for political office, seeking to run as the presidential candidate for the Costa Rican Renovation Party in 2021. However, his candidacy was rejected by the electoral authorities after the party failed to meet the necessary criteria required to file candidates.Costa Rica's Attorney General, Carlo Díaz, said that "silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society".

schema.headline: Gunmen kill Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez

title: So You Are: Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip
description: The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic. In a video
body: The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic. In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable"."Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online."He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said."So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body."That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body."We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that.""We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital."No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.

schema.headline: So You Are: Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip

title: Bilkis Bano: Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after Supreme Court bail for two convicts
description: The article has details that some readers may find disturbingA pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the
body: The article has details that some readers may find disturbingA pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back. The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap". On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken"."She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary." Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child. They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she'd told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.How a Gujarat riot victim stood up to her rapistsIndia Supreme Court cancels release of 2002 riots rapistsIndia PM Modi's government okayed rapists' releaseHer attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief"."I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said."For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again." Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives". "I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

schema.headline: Bilkis Bano: Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after Supreme Court bail for two convicts

title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
description: The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech
body: The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation. Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations". In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list. Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with ChinaIn the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred". They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

schema.headline: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed

title: Komyshuvakha: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after strikes that killed 57
description: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via
body: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty ImagesByMerlyn Thomas BBC Verify correspondent and Paul BrownBBC VerifyUkrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue. The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.Image source, DSNSImage caption, Emergency service vehicles have also been targetedOleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.Image source, DSNSOleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.Fears of second strike heard on police radiosLocal people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.Figure caption, Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in UkraineBodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.Image source, Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesTrevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures. His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.Image source, SBUImage caption, The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kitBall and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

schema.headline: Komyshuvakha: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after strikes that killed 57

title: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
description: Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia IrelandSarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv a
body: Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia IrelandSarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv and Ilya AbishevBBC News RussianUpdated 1 hour agoUkraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.A Kremlin spokesperson insisted the bridge would be rebuilt "better than before".Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating. The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry. Image source, EPAImage caption, There was heavy traffic in Kyiv on Tuesday after two major crossings were closed after strikes Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar. This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

schema.headline: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine

title: How Trump's chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in MayByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterAs US President Donald Trum
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in MayByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterAs US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of  data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market. But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.  This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".A blow to Asia's AI boomThis is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips. One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO. Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.  The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hubCountries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.The BBC has contacted Singapore, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".A headache for ChinaThe new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models. Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months."This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

schema.headline: How Trump's chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China

title: BBC launches educational show in Hausa for millions out of school in West Africa
description: BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West AfricaImage source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Hadiza l
body: BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West AfricaImage source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing houseworkByMadina MaishanuBBC AfricaReporting fromGoronyoAs she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school."Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village."They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married."It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains. Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home. Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Hadiza practises writing on the ground to make sure she doesn't forget the English alphabetHadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, After Rukayya's father was killed, she gave up school to earn money instead "It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat."If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube, externalSome attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Armed gangs, poverty and lack of funding all have a huge impact on children's education, says teacher Kamilu Sulaiman JakadaHe says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he says, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.Every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Many of Nigeria's schools face shortages of teachers, classrooms and learning materials after years of underfunding and lack of oversightMinister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been done… I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.She also says that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".In the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".Dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.

schema.headline: BBC launches educational show in Hausa for millions out of school in West Africa

title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does data show?
description: ByJake Horton, Thomas Copeland and Wesley StephensonBBC VerifyAlmost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes ar
body: ByJake Horton, Thomas Copeland and Wesley StephensonBBC VerifyAlmost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election. But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead. Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest stateHow did two Dan Sullivans end up in the race?Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.A New York Times story, external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed. "There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballotImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the voteHow does voting work in Alaska?Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference."There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:- Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.- Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) IncumbentThere was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.Image source, Alaska Division of ElectionsImage caption, A sample ballot for the US Senate election in AlaskaAs of Tuesday, Peltola holds 49.98% of the vote. In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Democrat Mary Peltola's said on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senatorWhat does ranked-choice voting data show so far?Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second. "The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."Additional reporting by Daniel Wainwright

schema.headline: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does data show?

title: Nvidia dismisses campaign to bring back Jensen Huang as Trump backs effort
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this yearByMichael Race and Osmond ChiaBusiness reportersUpda
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this yearByMichael Race and Osmond ChiaBusiness reportersUpdated 17 November 2026 02:37 GMTNvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon ValleyNew rulesThe Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US. He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad.The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to  companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry. US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost.Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump. 'A handshake with Jensen'Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation."Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Nvidia dismisses campaign to bring back Jensen Huang as Trump backs effort

title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
description: Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its l
body: Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Wednesday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.She has her alarm set for 0500, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is". She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.   This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers."As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said."Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include  banning players.GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither have Sony nor Microsoft.Louise Wooldridge from Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases."Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game."So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video. "The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter the cost or extra effort.

schema.headline: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6

title: Venâncio Mondlane: Mozambique opposition leader goes on trial amid tension in Maputo
description: Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly p
body: Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.Mondlane arrived at the Supreme Court early on Tuesday with "great peace of mind", and was greeted by dozens of supporters."As you can see, I arrive calm, confident in the work of my legal team," he told journalists gathered outside court, amid a heavy police presence.The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades."The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst. Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to  "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.

schema.headline: Venâncio Mondlane: Mozambique opposition leader goes on trial amid tension in Maputo

title: Suneung: Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
description: Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.The teach
body: Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul.  In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison."The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC."As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying."Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different.""I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again."Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day"."But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning."I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year."This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself."Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says."Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think."They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.There are difficult moments too.Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching."They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says."It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.He acknowledges these criticisms."Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."Of course, there  is no guarantee.Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison."He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."According to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he says."They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place."Additional reporting by Hosu Lee.

schema.headline: Suneung: Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
